fetched_contents.text: Aspirin in Ischemic Cerebrovascular Disease Abstract Background A vast consensus exists in defining a narrow range of recommended daily doses of aspirin, ie, 75 to 160 mg, for the prevention of myocardial infarction, stroke, and vascular death in patients with different manifestations of coronary heart disease. In contrast, for patients with cerebrovascular disease, a much larger degree of uncertainty still exists, with recommendations ranging from 30 to 1300 mg daily. Summary of Comment The contention that higher doses of aspirin (650 to 1300 mg) are more effective than lower doses in stroke prevention is based on indirect and selective comparisons of different trial data, mini-meta-analyses, or subgroup analyses of individual trials. In the absence of definitive evidence from direct randomized comparisons of low-dose versus high-dose aspirin in trials of adequate size to detect a moderate difference between the two, the biological hypotheses that underpin the suggestion of greater efficacy of higher aspirin doses in cerebrovascular disease patients are reviewed and disputed. Practical implications of the use of higher doses of aspirin are also assessed on the basis of theoretical calculations of absolute benefits and risks. Conclusions Until additional information from ongoing trials is available, good clinical practice should dictate the use of the lowest dose of aspirin shown effective in the prevention of stroke and death in patients with ischemic cerebrovascular disease, ie, 75 mg daily. Aspirin has well-characterized antiplatelet effects of proven clinical value.1 Probably no single cardiovascular drug has a database documenting its efficacy and safety comparable to that derived from more than 50 randomized aspirin trials.2 However, one unique feature of the clinical development of aspirin as an antiplatelet agent, ie, its “academia-driven” nature, has generated a long-standing debate on the “optimal” dose to prevent coronary and cerebral thrombosis. Traditionally, most drugs undergo “industry-driven” clinical development leading to the selection of one particular dose, based on phase II dose-finding studies, that is tested in a limited number of pivotal phase III studies of efficacy and safety. In the case of aspirin, a century-old drug, clinical testing of its antithrombotic efficacy was initiated largely on empirical grounds, and industry-driven clinical development was nil because, at the time, all commercial interest in the product had essentially vanished. Clinical trials were started mostly with doses in the range of 900 to 1500 mg daily, based on dose requirements for other established pharmacological effects of the drug (eg, analgesic) and/or dosing regimens dictated by coadministered drugs (ie, TID for dipyridamole, QID for sulfynpirazone). Soon thereafter, however, studies from academic centers altered this approach with the discovery that aspirin blocked prostaglandin synthesis3 by modifying a key enzyme of platelet arachidonate metabolism, ie, cyclooxygenase, also termed PGH synthase.4 These advances were instrumental in the development of analytical tools to quantitate the dose dependence and time dependence of the effects of aspirin on platelet biochemistry and function. A relatively simple tool, ie, the measurement of TXB2 during whole blood clotting,5 led to a clear understanding of the platelet effect of single oral aspirin doses in both health6 and disease.7 The cumulative effect of the drug in inhibiting platelet cyclooxygenase was also defined by studying the effect of low doses of aspirin given on a daily basis.6 8 This “academic” knowledge eventually led to a progressive reduction in the dose of aspirin used in clinical trials, down to the level of 30 mg daily.9 However, in the case of ischemic cerebrovascular disease and aspirin, questions remain concerning the use of higher versus lower doses of the drug. The debate waxes hot at times, generating strong words and prompting us to offer the following arguments in favor of using low-dose aspirin in patients who are prone to cerebrovascular thrombosis. Mechanism of Action Although several “cyclooxygenase-independent” actions of aspirin have been subsequently described,10 11 12 the effect of aspirin on cyclooxygenase has been exceptionally well defined and shown to involve the acetylation of a single amino acid residue (serine 529) in the polypeptide chain. This cyclooxygenase-dependent effect has several distinct features that are worth mentioning vis-à-vis other mechanisms. First, the aspirin-sensitive platelet cyclooxygenase enzyme has been identified, sequenced, and cloned.13 Second, this enzyme is responsible for the generation of a labile eicosanoid, TXA2,14 which amplifies the response of platelets to a variety of agonists.15 Third, increased TXA2 biosynthesis has been characterized in patients with acute coronary16 or cerebral17 ischemic syndromes as well as in conjunction with a variety of cardiovascular risk factors associated with enhanced thrombotic risk.18 Fourth, platelet cyclooxygenase is completely and permanently inhibited by aspirin, thus accounting for the persistent antiplatelet effect of a drug with a 15- to 20-minute half-life.19 Fifth, the dose requirement and single daily dosing for complete inactivation of platelet cyclooxygenase activity6 are consistent with the minimum effective dose of aspirin as an antithrombotic agent in a variety of disease states1 2 (Table 1). These five points imply that aspirin exerts its antithrombotic action by inhibiting platelet cyclooxygenase. None of these five features have been characterized for the cyclooxygenase-independent effects of aspirin on hemostasis. Although aspirin, in higher doses, acetylates a number of proteins besides platelet cyclooxygenase (eg, fibrinogen10 and prothrombin12 ), the dose-response relationship, duration, occurrence in the clinical setting, and relevance to the antithrombotic effect of aspirin have not been established.…

For patients receiving intravenous thrombolysis therapy, avoid antiplatelet therapy within the first 24 hours; antiplatelet therapy could then be initiated after brain imaging has excluded secondary hemorrhage [Evidence Level B]. 5. For transient ischemic attack or minor ischemic stroke patients who are being discharged from the emergency department, antiplatelet therapy should be started prior to discharge [Evidence Level C]. For ongoing antiplatelet therapy, refer to Section 6.2. Standard daily aspirin dose and clinical justification

The most commonly cited standard daily dose in the evidence is 81 mg, with other guideline ranges extending up to 325 mg daily, and with low-dose recommendations also mentioning 75 mg or 50–100 mg in some secondary-prevention contexts [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R5][N3-F3]. The evidence is not uniform: one source explicitly says that for patients with cerebrovascular disease, recommendations can range from 30 to 1300 mg daily, reflecting uncertainty and lack of definitive consensus [N1-R1]. But the best-supported modern consensus in the provided material is that low-dose aspirin is the preferred long-term secondary-prevention option, and that 81 mg is a commonly used dose [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-F3].

Aspirin is used after ischemic stroke because it is an antiplatelet agent that inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase, reducing the formation of thromboxane A2 and thereby lowering the risk of recurrent thrombotic events [N1-F1]. This mechanism is central to its clinical value in secondary stroke prevention. The evidence also notes that aspirin has well-characterized antiplatelet effects of proven clinical value and a long safety database [N1-F1]. In secondary prevention, aspirin is recommended for long-term use to reduce the risk of recurrent stroke and other vascular events unless there is an indication for anticoagulation [N1-F2][N3-F3]. A secondary-prevention checklist from the American Stroke Association similarly states that antiplatelet therapy is indicated in preference to oral anticoagulation in patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIA, and recommends aspirin 50–325 mg daily or clopidogrel 75 mg daily [N3-F3].

The guidelines and consensus statements that support this dose are mainly the Canadian Stroke Best Practices recommendations and related secondary-prevention guidance. The Canadian Stroke Best Practices source explicitly states that for long-term secondary stroke prevention, either acetylsalicylic acid (80 mg–325 mg daily), clopidogrel (75 mg daily), or combined aspirin and extended-release dipyridamole are appropriate treatment options [N1-F2]. It also says that for long-term secondary prevention, antiplatelet therapy should be started as soon as possible after brain imaging has excluded hemorrhage, and that dual antiplatelet therapy is recommended only in very specific patients [N1-F2]. The American Stroke Association secondary-stroke-prevention checklist similarly supports aspirin 50–325 mg daily as part of a broad antiplatelet-choice framework [N3-F3]. Overall, the evidence base is stronger for low-dose aspirin than for higher doses, and the safest clinical interpretation is that 81 mg is the most commonly cited standard daily dose in modern guidelines [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-F3].

The evidence is not uniform: one source explicitly says that for patients with cerebrovascular disease, recommendations can range from 30 to 1300 mg daily, reflecting uncertainty and lack of definitive consensus [N1-R1]. But the best-supported modern consensus in the provided material is that low-dose aspirin is the preferred long-term secondary-prevention option, and that 81 mg is a commonly used dose [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-F3].

Aspirin is used after ischemic stroke because it is an antiplatelet agent that inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase, reducing the formation of thromboxane A2 and thereby lowering the risk of recurrent thrombotic events [N1-F1]. This mechanism is central to its clinical value in secondary stroke prevention. The evidence also notes that aspirin has well-characterized antiplatelet effects of proven clinical value and a long safety database [N1-F1]. In secondary prevention, aspirin is recommended for long-term use to reduce the risk of recurrent stroke and other vascular events unless there is an indication for anticoagulation [N1-F2][N3-F3]. A secondary-prevention checklist from the American Stroke Association similarly states that antiplatelet therapy is indicated in preference to oral anticoagulation in patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIA, and recommends aspirin 50–325 mg daily or clopidogrel 75 mg daily [N3-F3].

The guidelines and consensus statements that support this dose are mainly the Canadian Stroke Best Practices recommendations and related secondary-prevention guidance. The Canadian Stroke Best Practices source explicitly states that for long-term secondary stroke prevention, either acetylsalicylic acid (80 mg–325 mg daily), clopidogrel (75 mg daily), or combined aspirin and extended-release dipyridamole are appropriate treatment options [N1-F2]. It also says that for long-term secondary prevention, antiplatelet therapy should be started as soon as possible after brain imaging has excluded hemorrhage, and that dual antiplatelet therapy is recommended only in very specific patients [N1-F2]. The American Stroke Association secondary-stroke-prevention checklist similarly supports aspirin 50–325 mg daily as part of a broad antiplatelet-choice framework [N3-F3]. Overall, the evidence base is stronger for low-dose aspirin than for higher doses, and the safest clinical interpretation is that 81 mg is the most commonly cited standard daily dose in modern guidelines [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-F3].

The Canadian Stroke Best Practices source says that for long-term secondary prevention, either **aspirin (80 mg–325 mg daily)**, **clopidogrel (75 mg daily)**, or **combined aspirin and extended-release dipyridamole** are appropriate treatment options [N1-F2]. It also notes that **dual antiplatelet therapy** is recommended for patients with **acute high-risk TIA or minor ischemic stroke of non-cardioembolic origin** for a short period, followed by monotherapy [N1-F2]. The secondary-stroke-prevention checklist similarly lists **clopidogrel 75 mg daily** and the combination of **aspirin 25 mg and extended-release dipyridamole 200 mg twice daily** as alternative options [N3-F3]. In addition, the evidence mentions newer short-term dual combinations such as **low-dose aspirin plus ticagrelor** [N1-F2]. So, in some patients, aspirin alone may not be the only option.

### 5) Practical advice for the patient
If you want to make sure you are taking the correct dose:
- **Ask your doctor directly**. The evidence shows that aspirin use and dose vary by clinical context and patient factors, so the safest route is to confirm with your physician [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-F3].
- **Do not assume 81 mg is automatically the correct dose for you**. The evidence supports individualized decision-making, so your dose may differ from the standard [N1-R1][N1-F2].
- **If you are unsure about your dose**, the best action is to ask your doctor and to avoid changing the dose on your own [N1-F1][N1-F2].
- **Be aware of bleeding risks**. The evidence notes that aspirin may increase bleeding risk, especially intracranial bleeding [N5-R2][N5-R5]. You should report any **unusual bleeding, bruising, or signs of bleeding risk** to your doctor immediately [N5-R2].

### 6) Bottom line
After an ischemic stroke, the **most commonly cited standard daily aspirin dose** in the evidence is **81 mg daily**, but the guidelines also allow for ranges up to **325 mg daily** and for individualized choices depending on patient factors and stroke subtype [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-F3]. The evidence supports aspirin because it is an effective antiplatelet agent for secondary stroke prevention, but it also emphasizes that dose may change and that alternative antiplatelet agents or combinations may be used in selected patients [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-F3]. So the clearest advice is:

> **Ask your doctor to confirm the dose for you. Do not assume the same dose applies to everyone.**

If you are unsure, the safest response is: **I want to make sure I am taking the right dose, so I will ask my doctor directly** [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-F3].
